hook: a book of focus asks where a wandering mind could possibly go

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vijnana Bhairava opened outward: the same knowing, lit in every seat on the bus. Today, it follows the mind when it wanders off.

Ninety seconds into a quiet sit, the mind has left the building. A quiz on Thursday. A text left on read. A chorus from middle school, on repeat. Then comes the sinking feeling, the one that says this is hopeless, I can't even sit still. So where exactly did it go? Here's the odd detail. The Vijnana Bhairava is a book of ways to steady the attention, and one of its verses asks that very question, then answers it with a puzzle of its own: where could the mind possibly go?
screen: `THE MIND LEAVES THE BUILDING.` → `THIS IS HOPELESS?` → `WHERE COULD IT GO?`

segments.voice: The verse runs like this, in plain words. Wherever the mind goes, outward or inward, there is Shiva's own state. And since he is everywhere, where can the mind go? The Sanskrit for that roaming mind is manas: the part that plans, replays and drifts. Now the puzzle. The doors so far ask the attention to stay put: rest at the turn of the breath, follow a sound to its end, catch a want at its flicker. This one lets the mind off the leash and follows it out. Why would a book of focus do that? Because of what it says Bhairava is. On the first day of this run, he told the Goddess his nature can't be pinned to any place or direction. If that's so, there's no outside to wander into. The quiz, the unanswered text, the old chorus: none of them, in the book's view, is somewhere the practice isn't. That doesn't make wandering the goal. It changes what noticing it means. The moment you see the mind has gone somewhere isn't a failure. It's the moment you woke up there. That's a sentence worth handing to anyone who says they're bad at meditating: in this book, the drifting mind is never outside the place it's looking for. So the puzzle solves itself: the mind can wander, but it can't leave.
screen: `WHEREVER IT GOES, SHIVA'S STATE.` · `THE OTHER DOORS SAY STAY PUT.` · `NO OUTSIDE TO WANDER INTO.` · `NOTICING IS WAKING UP.` · then, large: `IT CAN WANDER, BUT IT CAN'T LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the mind go wherever it likes, without herding it. Each time you notice where it's landed, don't drag it back; just recognize that you're aware there too, and let that recognition be the whole practice.
The Vijnana Bhairava: a book of doors. In this verse, a book that says the wandering mind has nowhere outside to go.
Keep this: the Vijnana Bhairava, where the mind can wander but can't leave. See you tomorrow.
